At the edge of the city, where the last apartment blocks gave way to weeds, there was a train station that no longer appeared on maps. Its sign had lost all but three letters, so travelers called it “The At.” Nobody knew what it had once been called. Perhaps it had been Ashford, or Watergate, or something grand like Imperial Terminus. Now it was only The At: a place of arrival without explanation.

Mara found it on a Tuesday, though the day had the colorless feeling of a Sunday afternoon. She had been walking for hours with a bag of oranges under one arm and a letter in her pocket that she had not opened. The letter was from her brother, who had left eleven years earlier and was believed, by the family, to be living somewhere coastal. Every winter he sent a card with a photograph of an ocean none of them recognized. Every winter, their mother cried in the kitchen and said, “He always hated the cold.”

The station waited behind a fence bent open by wind or boredom. Its clock had stopped at 4:17. A single platform stretched beneath a glass canopy webbed with cracks. Pigeons stood in the rafters like minor officials. There were benches with peeling green paint, a ticket window dark with dust, and a timetable so faded that every destination had become a gray smudge.

Mara entered because she had nowhere else to put the feeling in her chest.

Inside, there was an old man sweeping the platform with a broom made of twigs. He wore a blue railway cap and a coat too large for him. When he saw Mara, he did not look surprised.

“Are you waiting for someone?” he asked.

“I don’t know,” she said.

“Best kind of answer.”

He swept another small crescent of dust toward the tracks.

“Does a train come here?” Mara asked.

“Sometimes.”

“When?”

“When it has somewhere to go.”

This seemed unhelpful, but the old man said it with such confidence that Mara sat on a bench. She placed the oranges beside her. The letter in her pocket seemed to gain weight.

Across the tracks stood a field of tall grass, silvered by the lowering sun. Beyond it, the city rose in distant pieces: cranes, towers, smoke from restaurant vents, the blinking red lights of aircraft warning beacons. From here, the city looked almost gentle. Its noise arrived softened, like the memory of a crowd.

The old man stopped sweeping.

“You’ve got a letter,” he said.

Mara looked down.

“Everybody who comes here has one. Some keep it in pockets. Some carry it in their faces. One woman had hers tattooed on her wrist, though she said she couldn’t read it.”

“Do people open them here?”

“Some do. Most don’t. Opening is not the difficult part.”

Mara took out the envelope. Her brother’s handwriting leaned forward, impatient and narrow. It was addressed to her, not their mother. That alone had frightened her. Their brother wrote to their mother because that was the agreement. He sent postcards and seasonal excuses, small parcels of proof that he remained alive. He did not write private letters.

The envelope had been in Mara’s mailbox for six days.

“What happens if I open it?” she asked.

The old man leaned on his broom. “You’ll know what it says.”

“That’s not what I mean.”

“No,” he said. “It never is.”

A sound drifted through the evening: not quite a whistle, not quite wind. The pigeons lifted all at once, turning beneath the broken canopy in a gray spiral. Somewhere far down the track, a light appeared.

Mara stood.

The train approached without noise. It had no visible engine, only three silver carriages gliding through the grass-darkening twilight. Its windows shone warmly. For a moment, Mara saw faces inside: a girl holding a bouquet of dead flowers; a man in a wedding suit; a boy asleep against a suitcase; a woman laughing alone. Then the train slowed and stopped precisely beneath the broken clock.

The doors opened.

No conductor stepped out. No one called a destination. The interior smelled faintly of rain, cedarwood, and dust from old books.

The old man gave Mara a small nod.

“Does it go to the coast?” she asked.

“It goes where you cannot remain,” he said.

That was the closest thing to an answer she had received all day.

Mara picked up the bag of oranges, then set it down again. It seemed ridiculous to take oranges on a mysterious train. It seemed more ridiculous to leave them. Finally, she took one from the bag and placed the rest on the bench.

“For you,” she told the old man.

“I prefer apples,” he said, but he smiled.

She climbed aboard.

Inside, the carriage was almost empty. The seats were upholstered in dark red fabric, worn smooth in the middle. Above each seat hung a small brass lamp. Mara chose a window seat. As the doors closed, she saw the old man on the platform lift one orange from the bag and inspect it as though it were a rare machine.

Then the train moved.

The station slid backward. The field blurred. The city’s distant lights stretched into gold threads, then disappeared behind a rise of dark trees.

Mara sat very still.

Across the aisle, the girl with the dead flowers watched her. She looked about sixteen, though grief had given her the careful expression of someone much older.

“First time?” the girl asked.

“Yes.”

“Don’t worry,” she said. “Nobody knows where they’re going. They only know why they got on.”

Mara nodded, pretending this made sense.

She held the letter in both hands. The envelope seemed warm now, as if it had been near a fire. Outside, the landscape changed too quickly to name: a river beneath moonlight, a row of childhood houses, a forest full of white birds, an empty playground turning slowly in snow.

At last, Mara tore the envelope open.

Her brother’s letter was short.

It said: I am coming home. I am afraid you will not recognize me. I am afraid I will recognize myself. Please meet me at the old station, if it still exists. Tuesday. 4:17.

There was no date.

Mara read it twice. Then a third time, because letters are different after the first reading; they become smaller, crueler, more exact.

The train began to slow.

Outside the window stood the old station again, bright beneath a morning sky. The clock still read 4:17. On the platform, a man waited with one hand in the pocket of a weather-beaten coat. He was older than the brother Mara remembered. Of course he was. His hair was touched with gray. His shoulders had become uncertain. But he held himself with the same slight forward lean as the handwriting on the envelope.

Mara stepped onto the platform.

For a moment, neither of them moved.

Then her brother said, “I wasn’t sure you’d come.”

Mara looked back at the train, but it had already become only mist on the tracks.

“I wasn’t sure either,” she said.

The old man had vanished. The bag of oranges was gone. The station sign, above them, seemed almost readable in the morning light.

Her brother opened his arms.

Mara walked toward him, carrying the letter between them like a small, opened door.
